title: How much of a water-leak detector's score on the BattLeDIM benchmark beats random alarms?
lede: research programme: leak detection on the real BattLeDIM L-Town benchmark (2018 tunes, 2019 tests), scored against chance; a residual CUSUM finds 13 of the 19 leaks that start in 2019 and an automatic reimplementation of the published LILA method 14 (1 false alarm), against a median 11 for the same 26 random alarms (P = 0.105 and 0.019, the latter back to 0.265 under a different tie-break); the alarming sensor is within 300 m of the leak for 5 and 7 of them against a chance median of 0 (P < 0.001), and LILA's released code dates leaks it is told about rather than detecting them blind; minimum night flow on the district meter finds only 3 of the 9 leaks under 12 m³/h (pressure CUSUM 7), because night flow swings by about 11 m³/h from night to night; halving that swing with a weekday baseline and the 82 smart meters still finds 3, and the pressure detectors' hits on the slow-ramp leaks came when those leaked 0.01 to 0.22 m³/h, so they were luck
summary: An open research programme on leak detection and localisation in water distribution networks, run on the one public benchmark with a realistic network, two years of SCADA data and a published leak schedule: BattLeDIM's L-Town (Vrachimis et al. 2022; Zenodo 4017659, CC-BY-4.0), which infra-waterloss could not reach and replaced with Net3. It asks how much of a detector's reported skill is above what random alarms would score, and whether a data-driven detector can carry a false-alarm rate fixed before the year is seen. Step 1 (2026-11-12) builds the harness: SHA-256-checked loader, ground truth from the leak-flow files (onsets match Melnikov 2025's table), matching (an alarm counts for the running leak with the latest onset within 30 days) and distances along the pipe graph. Detector D1 fits each of the 33 pressure sensors on hour-of-week, tank level and the three inlet flows over a trailing two-week window ending a week back, runs a one-sided CUSUM on the standardised residuals, and re-anchors its window after each alarm (an earlier hold-off version re-alarmed on the same leak; a unit test caught it). Tuned on 2018 only (at most 2 false alarms), on 2019 it detects 13 of the 19 new leaks with 2 false alarms, a median delay of 104 h (11 to 341), and 16 of BattLeDIM's 23 counting the 3 of 4 carried-over leaks it found in 2018; without localisation, so not comparable with the published 15 to 17 of 23, which required a reported pipe within 300 m. Against the same 26 alarms placed at random (1,000 draws, 14 days apart, random sensors), the detection count is near chance (median 11, 95% range 8 to 13, P = 0.105), as is detection within 72 h (4 against 2, P = 0.145); but the alarming sensor is within 300 m along the pipes of 5 detected leaks against a chance median of 0 (P < 0.001). L-Town is a simulated network with simulated leaks; 2018 labels were used for tuning, which competitors did not have; nothing here is an operational recommendation. Step 2 (2026-11-12) reimplements LILA's identification (Daniel et al. 2022: pairwise sensor regressions on the inlet flow, a most-affected-sensor reconstruction error, Montgomery's CUSUM) and runs it blind on D1's trailing window; the authors' released notebook instead writes in each known leak's sensor and calibration windows. Tuned on 2018 (delta 1, Cthr 20), it detects 14 of 19 with 1 false alarm and 26 alarms: P = 0.019 against chance on the count, which refutes the programme's pre-registered H1 as written, but thinly: 2 of the 13 settings with 20 or more alarms clear 0.05, and a disclosed post-hoc change of the most-affected-sensor tie-break (ties occur in 46% of hours, because the inlet flow drives every sensor) gives 13 of 19 and P = 0.265. Its most affected sensor is within 300 m of 7 of the 14 leaks (chance median 0, P < 0.001), and every one of the 27 settings beats chance on that count. Zenodo was unreachable; the inputs came from public GitHub copies whose SHA-256s match Zenodo's. Step 6 (2026-11-13) tests the practitioner's minimum-night-flow statistic on the district water balance (p227 + p235 less the tank T1's storage change, least hourly flow from 00:00 to 06:00, a CUSUM on its trailing median and MAD), pre-registered as hypothesis H4: that it detects incipient leaks sooner than pressure CUSUM. Tuned on 2018 the same way, it detects 3 of the 9 new 2019 leaks under 12 m³/h, against 7 for D1 and 7 for LILA, and is earlier than D1 on 1 of them: H4 refuted. The nightly minimum's two-week robust sd is 10.7 m³/h, the size of the leaks; a post-hoc look shows Friday and Saturday nights 10 to 15 m³/h above the week, and removing that pattern leaves 7.1 m³/h. Over all 19 new leaks it finds 10 with 6 false alarms, at chance on the count (P = 0.80). Step 7 (2026-11-13) runs the two fixes step 6 named, pre-registered: a 2018 weekday profile and the night balance net of the 82 AMR meters (8.2% of district flow). Together they halve the night-to-night spread to 5.1 m³/h, yet the combined statistic still detects 3 of the 9 small leaks (AMR-net alone: 6 of 9, median delay 473 h): H4 refuted again. The ground-truth leak flows show why: five of the nine are ramps leaking under 0.5 m³/h for a week and 1.3 to 6 m³/h at day 30, invisible to any trailing-baseline statistic inside the 30-day match; and the pressure detectors were credited with four of them at the hour the leak carried 0.01 to 0.22 m³/h, chance matches rather than detections. A detection-only score should credit an alarm only once the leak's flow passes a stated level.
